contraception.question: Can I get birth control even though I'm a teenager?
contraception.answer: Health services for young people are meant to be confidential. The rules on parental consent for under-18s can differ by service, so a health worker can explain what applies to you. Specific service or legal requirements may vary by setting.
contraception.evidenceClaim: WHO recommends adolescent SRH services, including contraceptive information and services, without mandatory parental/guardian authorization or notification.
contraception.conditions: Consent wording is interim pending legal review (Children Act 2022 s.16(1)).

contraception.question: Do I need my parents' permission to get contraception?
contraception.answer: Health services for young people are meant to be confidential. The rules on parental consent for under-18s can differ by service, so a health worker can explain what applies to you.
contraception.conditions: Exact legal age of consent under current Kenyan law not established by available sources — flagged, not stated. Consent wording is interim pending legal review (Children Act 2022 s.16(1)).

contraception.question: Which birth control methods can a teenager use?
contraception.answer: Kenya's 2025 family planning guideline says adolescents and youth can safely use any contraceptive method that follows the guideline and the medical eligibility criteria. A health worker will help you choose and will explain the possible side effects, because teenagers may find side effects harder to put up with. Using condoms as well gives protection from STIs and HIV.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Adolescents and youth in need of contraceptive services can safely use any method that follows the guideline and MEC criteria." / "Adolescents may be less tolerant of side effects. Healthcare providers shall explain the possible side effects during counselling…" / "Adolescents and youth shall be sensitized on the use of condoms for dual protection against pregnancy and STI/HIV."
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "FP Services for Adolescents and Youth", p. 25; WHO, Family Planning: A Global Handbook for Providers (2022), Ch. 1, p. 5
contraception.conditions: Medical conditions can change which method suits a girl. No consent rule is stated here (see open issue).
contraception.safetyNotes: A health worker should confirm the choice, especially if she has a medical condition or might already be pregnant.

contraception.question: Do I still need a condom if I'm on the pill or the implant?
contraception.answer: Yes, if you want protection from STIs. WHO says condoms are the only contraceptive method that prevents both pregnancy and STIs, including HIV, and Kenya's 2025 guideline says condoms offer dual protection. Other methods prevent pregnancy only, so young people are encouraged to use condoms as well.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Male and female condoms help prevent both pregnancy and most STIs (including HIV)…" / "Therefore, condoms offer dual protection against unintended pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV." / "Adolescents and youth shall be sensitized on the use of condoms for dual protection against pregnancy and STI/HIV." WHO: condoms are the only method that prevents both pregnancy and STIs.
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Male condom", p. 173 and p. 25; WHO, Family planning/contraception methods fact sheet (3 July 2025)
contraception.conditions: Protection depends on using condoms every time and correctly. Step-by-step use is not included (needs the full table on pp. 176 to 178 and a clinician).
contraception.safetyNotes: If a condom breaks or slips, or she has had unprotected sex, she should see a health worker promptly (see NEW-C-06, on hold). She should also go for any STI symptoms.

contraception.question: Will contraception make me infertile or stop me having babies later?
contraception.answer: No. WHO states that modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility. Kenya's 2025 guideline says fertility comes back fairly quickly after you stop: on average it can take 3 to 6 months for most methods, and sometimes up to 12 months after the injection. If it takes much longer, a health worker can look for other causes.
contraception.evidenceClaim: WHO: modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility. "After stopping a contraceptive, a woman may expect an average of 3 to 6 months delay in returning to fertility for most methods and sometimes up to 12 months for DMPA." / "In cases of prolonged delay in the return to fertility, underlying causes of female sub-fertility or infertility may need to be considered…"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Return to fertility after contraception", p. 31; WHO, Family planning/contraception methods fact sheet (2025); WHO, Family Planning Handbook (2022), Ch. 1, p. 3
contraception.conditions: The same guideline says return is "immediate" for progestin-only pills (p. 74) and the IUCD (p. 134) and gives other figures for injectables (pp. 96, 108), so no per-method figures are given. Does not cover infertility caused by untreated STIs.
contraception.safetyNotes: If she is worried about her fertility, or has pelvic pain or unusual discharge, she should see a health worker.

contraception.question: Is irregular bleeding normal with the implant or the injection?
contraception.answer: Light spotting or irregular bleeding is common with both. The guideline says it is common with the injection, especially in the first 6 to 8 months, and with the implant, especially in the first year. It says this is not harmful and usually does not need treatment. If the bleeding keeps going or worries you, see a health worker.
contraception.evidenceClaim: Injectables: "Spotting or light bleeding is common during use of injectable contraceptives, particularly during the first 6-8 months of use. It is not harmful. Reassure the client." / "If the bleeding is persistent, assess for gynaecological problems and treat accordingly". Implant: "Reassure client that light bleeding/spotting is common in women using this method especially in the first year. It is not serious and usually does not require treatment." / "If the bleeding is persistent assess for gynaecological problems and treat accordingly".
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), Table 4.14 (injectables) p. 105; Table 4.20 (implants) p. 117
contraception.conditions: Drug treatments listed in the tables are not included. Heavy bleeding is not covered by these rows.
contraception.safetyNotes: Persistent or heavy bleeding, pain, or a late period with a possible pregnancy need a health worker.

contraception.question: How does the contraceptive implant work, and how long does it last?
contraception.answer: The implant is one or two small rods that a trained health worker places under the skin of your upper arm. It slowly releases a hormone that prevents pregnancy. Kenya's 2025 guideline says it is 99.9% effective and starts working 24 hours after it is put in. Depending on the type, it lasts 3 or 5 years. Changes in your bleeding are common, such as spotting or longer or missing periods. It does not protect against STIs, so use condoms too if you are at risk. Only a trained health worker can put it in and take it out.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Implants provide 99.9% effective protection against pregnancy. They are effective 24 hours post insertion." / Table 4.17: Jadelle, 2 rods, 5 years; Implanon and Implanon NXT, 1 rod, 3 years; Levoplant, 2 rods, 3 years. / "The client cannot initiate or discontinue the method on her own as it requires a trained healthcare provider to insert and remove the implant" / "Insertion and removal require minor surgical procedures and may be uncomfortable" / "Change in menstrual pattern including; amenorrhoea, spotting, intermenstrual bleeding or prolonged bleeding." / "Do not protect against STIs, including hepatitis B and HIV. Individuals at risk should use condoms in addition to the implants."
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Contraceptive implants", pp. 109 to 110 (Table 4.17 on p. 109)
contraception.conditions: Brand names are left out. Some medicines (some HIV medicines, for example) can make implants work less well (p. 109 key messages); not included. Side effects such as headache, nausea and mood changes are not listed. Fertility after removal is not stated because the guideline contradicts itself (see conflicts above).
contraception.safetyNotes: A health worker must confirm that the implant suits her and that she is not pregnant. Pain, redness or swelling at the arm, or very heavy bleeding, needs a clinic visit (not stated in the pages read; ask the clinician to confirm this line or remove it).

contraception.question: How does the contraceptive injection work, and how often do I need it?
contraception.answer: The injection is given by a health worker. The most common kind is given every three months (13 weeks); another kind is given every two months. Kenya's 2025 guideline says it is 99% effective if you get each injection on time, and that the risk of pregnancy is highest when you are late or miss one. Changes in bleeding are common: irregular, heavy or long bleeding, light spotting, or no periods at all. After you stop, it can take longer to get pregnant than with most other methods: four months or longer, and sometimes up to 12 months. It does not protect against STIs, so use condoms too if you are at risk.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Given every three months (13 weeks)" (DMPA) and "Given every two months" (NET-EN), Table 4.11. / "Effectiveness depends on receiving injections on time. Risk of pregnancy is greatest when a woman is late for or misses an injection." / "POIC is 99% effective if used correctly and consistently" / Side effects include "irregular bleeding", "heavy and prolonged bleeding", "light spotting or bleeding", "amenorrhoea, especially after one year of use". / "Return of fertility may be delayed for four months or longer after discontinuation" / "sometimes up to 12 months for DMPA" / "They offer no protection against STIs, including hepatitis B and HIV; individuals at risk for these should use condoms in addition to injectable contraceptives"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Injectable contraceptives", p. 94 (Table 4.11); p. 95 (effectiveness); p. 96 (limitations and side effects); p. 32 (return to fertility, up to 12 months for DMPA)
contraception.conditions: No age is stated (see conflict 1 above). The self-injected kind (DMPA-SC) is not covered. The grace period for late injections is not given. Return-to-fertility wording now matches NEW-C-03 and NEW-C-21 (four months or longer, sometimes up to 12 months); the guideline's own figures vary (pp. 31, 96, 108), and the combined injectable is given as about 5 months.
contraception.safetyNotes: If she is late for an injection and has had unprotected sex, she should see a health worker soon (a held-topic area; do not build more detail without a clinician).

contraception.question: How does the combined contraceptive pill work, and what are the side effects?
contraception.answer: The combined pill has two hormones and is taken once a day, ideally at the same time every day. Kenya's 2025 guideline says it is 99.7% effective if used correctly and consistently. The risk of pregnancy is highest if you start a new pack 3 or more days late or miss 3 or more pills near the start or end of a pack. Mild side effects such as nausea, spotting between periods, headaches, breast tenderness and mood or weight changes are common, especially in the first three months. Severe vomiting or diarrhoea, and some medicines (for example some TB, epilepsy and HIV medicines), can make it work less well, so tell the health worker. The pill does not protect against STIs. If you miss pills, ask a health worker what to do, because it depends on how many you missed and when.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "COCs are 99.7% effective in preventing pregnancy if used correctly and consistently." / "The risk of pregnancy is greatest when a woman starts a new pill pack 3 or more days late, or misses 3 or more pills near the beginning or the end of a pill pack." / "COCs must be taken daily to be effective, preferably at the same time each day." / "Contraceptive effectiveness could also be lowered in the presence of gastroenteritis, severe vomiting, and diarrhoea." / "Effectiveness may be lowered if the client is on anti-TB drugs" / "Nausea (more common in the first three months)" / "COCs do not offer protection against STls, including hepatitis B and HIV." / MEC Category 1: "Age: from menarche to 40 years"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Combined Oral Contraceptive (COCs) Pills", p. 58 (what it is); p. 59 (effectiveness, first limitations); p. 60 (limitations, side effects); p. 61 (eligibility)
contraception.conditions: Missed-pill instructions are conditional tables (Table 4.4, p. 72) and are not summarised here (see appendix to `kb-candidates-2025-fp-guideline.md`). Serious but rare side effects (blood clots, stroke) are listed on p. 60 and are not included without a clinician. The pill does not suit everyone (medical conditions change eligibility).
contraception.safetyNotes: A health worker should check that the pill is suitable. Severe chest pain, a very bad headache, or a swollen painful leg need urgent care (not stated in the pages read; the clinician should decide whether to add warning signs).

contraception.question: If a boy pulls out before he finishes, can I still get pregnant?
contraception.answer: Yes. Pulling out (withdrawal) is one of the least effective ways to prevent pregnancy. Kenya's family planning guideline says that as people commonly use it, about 20 out of 100 women whose partners use withdrawal become pregnant in the first year. Even when it is done correctly every time, about 4 out of 100 become pregnant. It does not protect against STIs. A health worker can help you choose a more reliable method.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "one of the least effective methods, as commonly used" [...] "about 20 out of 100 women whose partners use withdrawal will become pregnant in the first year" [...] "about 4 out of 100 women whose partners use withdrawal will become pregnant in the first year" [...] "It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), "Withdrawal Method (Coitus Interruptus)", p. 202
contraception.conditions: The guideline does not mention pre-ejaculate (precum), so the answer does not either. The sentence about a health worker choosing a more reliable method is a referral note and is not stated in the page read.
contraception.safetyNotes: If she had sex without protection and is worried, she should see a health worker (see the held entry on emergency contraception).

contraception.question: How well do condoms work, and how do I use one correctly?
contraception.answer: Kenya's family planning guideline says male condoms are 87% effective as people typically use them, and 98% effective when used correctly and every time. They also help protect against most STIs, including HIV. Use a new condom for every act of sex, check the packet is not torn or past its expiry date, unroll it all the way down the erect penis, and hold the rim while pulling out. Never reuse a condom, and do not use oil-based lubricants. Do not throw a used condom in a flush toilet.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "male condoms are 87% effective in typical use and much more effective, at 98%, when used correctly and consistently" [...] "Male and female condoms help prevent both pregnancy and most STIs (including HIV)" [...] "A new condom must be worn for each act of sexual intercourse" [...] "not use it if it is torn, damaged" [...] "past the expiration date" [...] "Cannot be used with oil-based lubricants" [...] "Condoms should not be reused" [...] "Do not dispose of the condom in a flush toilet"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), "Male condom", pp. 173 to 174 (mode of action, effectiveness, limitations); "Condom use and disposal", pp. 176 to 178 (Table 7.1 and the do-not list)
contraception.conditions: The guideline describes use for a man's condom; the steps are shortened. Pages are printed pages inferred from the page footers and should be rechecked.
contraception.safetyNotes: If a condom breaks or slips, she should see a health worker straight away. That case is the held entry NEW-C-06 and is not answered here.

contraception.question: What is a female condom, and does it work?
contraception.answer: A female condom is a thin sheath that you wear inside the vagina. It has a ring at each end, and the open ring stays outside. Kenya's family planning guideline says it is slightly less effective than the male condom, about 79% to 95% effective. It can be put in up to eight hours before sex, it cannot be reused, and used properly and every time it helps protect against STIs, including HIV.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Effectiveness ranges from 79% to 95%" [...] "It can be inserted eight hours before an anticipated sexual act" [...] "Cannot be reused" [...] "With consistent and proper use, condoms are highly effective for prevention against STIs, including HIV/AIDS" [...] "the ring at the open end holds the condom outside the vagina"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), "Female condom", p. 180
contraception.conditions: The guideline also says female condoms are expensive; this is not in the answer. Where to get one is not in the page read.
contraception.safetyNotes: If a condom slips or breaks, see a health worker (held entry NEW-C-06).

contraception.question: What is an IUD (the coil), and how long does it last?
contraception.answer: An IUD is a small, flexible plastic device that a trained health worker puts inside the womb to prevent pregnancy. Kenya's family planning guideline says copper devices protect for as long as 12 years and hormone devices for 5 years, and that they are 99% effective when used correctly. Fertility returns right away when it is taken out. Bleeding changes are common but not harmful. An IUD does not protect against STIs or HIV. For girls under 18 who have never had a baby, the guideline says an IUD can generally be provided after careful counselling on the range of methods, with follow-up, because the device is more likely to come out and there is a concern about STIs.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "small flexible plastic device" [...] "inserted into the uterine cavity to" [...] "Return to fertility is immediate" [...] "As long as 12 years" [...] "IU(C)D are 99% effective if used correctly and consistently" [...] "Does not offer protection against STI/HIV transmission" [...] "Requires a trained healthcare provider for insertion and removal" [...] "Generally, provide after" [...] "careful counselling on" [...] "increased risk of IU(C)D expulsion" [...] "Ensure follow-up."
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), Chapter 5 "Intrauterine (Contraceptive) Devices", pp. 134 to 135 (what it is, duration, effectiveness); p. 137 (limitations); Table 5.3 Category 2 conditions, p. 140 (younger than 18 and nulliparity); p. 154 (where it is provided)
contraception.conditions: The age rule is a medical eligibility category 2 (benefits usually outweigh risks) and is a decision for the health worker. The guideline does not say a girl needs a parent's consent. Page numbers are printed pages inferred from the footers.
contraception.safetyNotes: Only a trained health worker can fit or remove an IUD, so she should see a health worker for choice, fitting and removal.

contraception.question: I missed my injection date. What should I do?
contraception.answer: Go back to the clinic, however long it has been since your appointment. Kenya's family planning guideline says that a woman who misses her injection should come back to the clinic regardless of how much time has passed. A health worker will tell you what to do next.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "she fails to keep the appointment date, she should be encouraged to come back to the clinic, regardless of how much time has passed since the missed appointment"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), "Missed appointments" (injectable contraceptives), p. 106
contraception.conditions: The page read does not say whether she could already be pregnant or how long the protection lasts. The last sentence about a health worker is a referral note not stated in the page.
contraception.safetyNotes: If she had sex without protection after the missed date, she should see a health worker soon. Emergency contraception is a held topic.

contraception.question: Can birth control make me gain or lose weight?
contraception.answer: Kenya's family planning guideline lists weight change as a possible side effect of the combined pill, the hormonal injection and the implant. It does not say how much weight, and it does not say who is affected. If a side effect worries you, talk to a health worker.
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), combined oral contraceptives side effects, p. 60; injectable side effects, p. 96; implants side effects, p. 111
contraception.conditions: The guideline lists weight change among the side effects of these methods but gives no amounts, so the answer cannot say how likely or how large. The talk-to-a-health-worker line is a referral note.
contraception.safetyNotes: Sudden or severe weight change with other symptoms needs a health worker.

contraception.question: Can I use the pill, injection or implant if I have never had a baby?
contraception.answer: Yes. Kenya's family planning guideline says you can use combined pills, the injection, the implant and the female condom even if you have never had a baby. For the combined pill it lists ages from your first period up to 40 years. A health worker will check which method is right for your age and health.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Age: from menarche to 40 years" [...] "Women of any parity (parous and nulliparous)" [...] "All women of reproductive age, of any parity, including nulliparous women"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), combined pill eligibility, p. 61; injectable eligibility, p. 97; implants eligibility, p. 111; female condom eligibility, p. 181
contraception.conditions: The medical eligibility categories can change this for a girl with a medical condition. Whether she needs a parent's consent is not stated here (see the consent question for the clinicians).
contraception.safetyNotes: A health worker should check eligibility, especially for a girl with a medical condition or who might be pregnant.

contraception.question: I am breastfeeding. Which contraception can I use?
contraception.answer: Breastfeeding can protect against pregnancy for a while, but only if three things are all true. Kenya's family planning guideline calls this the breastfeeding method (LAM, the lactational amenorrhoea method): your periods have not come back, your baby is fed only on breast milk, and your baby is under six months old. Used this way it is up to 98% effective. When any one of the three stops being true, you need another family planning method straight away. A health worker can tell you which methods are safe while you breastfeed.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "The woman's menstrual periods have not resumed" [...] "The baby is exclusively breastfed" [...] "The baby is less than six months old" [...] "LAM is up to 98% effective if practiced during an exclusive breastfeeding period" [...] "When any of these three criteria is no longer met, another FP method must be introduced in a timely manner"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), Chapter 8 "Lactational Amenorrhoea Method (LAM)", pp. 186 to 187
contraception.conditions: The page read covers LAM only. The guideline also gives rules for other methods after childbirth (for example, the combined pill has restrictions while breastfeeding), but this entry does not list them. The last sentence is a referral note and is not stated on the page.
contraception.safetyNotes: A girl who has just had a baby should see a health worker about her method, because some methods are not suitable in the first months.

contraception.question: Does birth control cause cancer?
contraception.answer: Kenya's family planning guideline lists protection against cancer of the ovary and of the lining of the womb as a benefit of combined pills, and says the progestin-only pill (a pill with one hormone) may help prevent cancer of the lining of the womb. It lists a family history of breast cancer among the conditions in which a woman can still use the combined pill. It says women who have breast cancer, or have had it, should generally not use the progestin-only pill. Tell the health worker about any cancer in you or your close family so they can help you choose.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Protection against ovarian and endometrial cancer" [...] "May prevent endometrial cancer" [...] "Category 1" [...] "Benign breast disease, or family history of breast cancer" [...] "Women who have breast cancer or a history of breast cancer"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), combined oral contraceptives benefits, p. 59; COC eligibility, Category 1 list, p. 61; progestin-only pills benefits, p. 74; POP conditions, p. 81
contraception.conditions: The pages read do not say whether hormonal methods change the risk of breast cancer in a healthy woman, so this answer does not say they cause it or that they are safe for it. The guideline's list of side effects was not searched for the word cancer in full. The last sentence is a referral note. The clinicians should decide how to word the breast cancer part.
contraception.safetyNotes: Any breast lump should be seen by a health worker.

contraception.question: Can I stop or change my contraceptive method, and how soon can I get pregnant after I stop?
contraception.answer: Yes, you can ask to stop or change your method. Kenya's family planning guideline says health workers must counsel anyone who wants to stop on how to switch in good time, so you do not get pregnant when you do not want to. An implant can be taken out any time you want. Most methods let you get pregnant again fairly soon, but the guideline says it can take about 3 to 6 months for most methods and up to 12 months after the injection. If side effects bother you, tell the health worker, because another method may suit you better.
contraception.evidenceClaim: "Healthcare providers have a duty to adequately counsel clients wishing to discontinue contraception about timely method-switching" [...] "implants can be removed anytime the client desires" [...] "a fairly prompt return of fertility after discontinuation" [...] "an average of 3 to 6 months delay in returning to fertility for most methods and sometimes up to 12 months for DMPA" [...] "Discontinuation or switch due to side effects"
contraception.source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (2025), "Return to fertility after contraception" and discontinuation, p. 32; implants follow-up, p. 116
contraception.conditions: Fertility returning 'fairly soon' and the 3 to 6 month figure appear together in the guideline; this answer says both. The last sentence about side effects is a referral note.
contraception.safetyNotes: If she stops a method and does not want to be pregnant, she should start another method straight away or use condoms.

sti.question: I might have been exposed to HIV. Is there something I can take to stop it?
sti.answer: Yes — post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a course of medication started as soon as possible after exposure. Both Kenyan and WHO guidance agree it should be started within 72 hours, since it becomes less effective the longer you wait.
sti.evidenceClaim: PEP (28-day ARV regimen) must be initiated within 72 hours of exposure per both sources — this is one of the few points of full agreement between MoH and WHO.
sti.source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Annex 1, pp. 26–28 and WHO (2018), Ch. 7 §7.3.5/7.3.14, pp. 43, 46
sti.conditions: Specific drug names/dosing not established by sources — do not include in the answer.
sti.safetyNotes: Must direct to immediate facility-based care — this is time-critical.

sti.question: I have unusual discharge, itching, burning or lower belly pain. Could it be an STI?
sti.answer: It could be, but unusual discharge can have other causes too, and only a test can tell which. Many STIs cause no symptoms at all. Kenya's 2026 guidelines now prefer lab tests that find the exact infection before treatment, so ask for a test at a health facility. Lower belly pain, pain during sex or bleeding between periods needs a visit soon, because untreated infections can spread to the womb and tubes.
sti.evidenceClaim: Laboratory-confirmed (aetiological) diagnosis is the preferred approach to STI care in Kenya. Chlamydia symptoms in women include abnormal vaginal discharge, pain on passing urine, and bleeding after sex or between periods; gonorrhoea in women may cause abnormal discharge and lower abdominal discomfort. Untreated infection can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy and infertility.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.3.1 p. 161; s. 3.5.1 Chlamydia p. 171; s. 3.5.2 Gonorrhoea p. 171; WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet
sti.conditions: Where a facility has no laboratory, the guideline still allows clinical diagnosis (s. 3.3.2 p. 162). No treatment or drug advice is given. The 2018 guideline (the earlier source) was replaced by the 2026 edition; the privacy sentence that came from it is dropped.
sti.safetyNotes: Lower belly pain with fever, or pain during sex, needs a clinic visit soon. She should not self-treat.

sti.question: Can STIs be cured, and can they harm me if I leave them?
sti.answer: Four common STIs (syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis) can be cured with antibiotics. HIV and herpes cannot be cured, but medicine can keep them under control. Some untreated infections can spread and cause pelvic inflammatory disease, so it is better to get tested and treated early.
sti.evidenceClaim: WHO: syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis are curable; HIV and herpes are not but can be managed. Kenya 2026: untreated chlamydia and gonorrhoea can ascend to cause PID, ectopic pregnancy and infertility; testing finds the exact infection.
sti.source: WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet; Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.3.1 p. 161; s. 3.5.1 and 3.5.2 p. 171
sti.conditions: The curable and not-curable statements rest on the WHO fact sheet only; IG2026 pages read do not state curability. Being cured does not protect against catching the infection again. Partner treatment is not included. The 2018 guideline citation is dropped.
sti.safetyNotes: She should go to a clinic for testing and treatment rather than self-treating.

sti.question: Is the HPV vaccine available to me, and am I old enough?
sti.answer: Kenya's 2026 HIV and STI guideline says the HPV vaccine is available in Kenya for girls aged 9 to 14, and since November 2025 it is given as a single dose. If you are older than that, ask at a government health facility whether you can still get it.
sti.evidenceClaim: Kenya's HPV programme targets 10-year-old girls and moved from a two-dose to a single-dose schedule in November 2025. IG2026 (p. 182) adds that the HPV vaccine is highly effective for preventing genital warts, but does not state who is eligible.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.5.2.5, p. 57; WHO AFRO, Kenya transitions to single-dose HPV vaccination schedule (page dated 1 November 2025)
sti.conditions: Sources disagree on the target age (WHO AFRO: 10-year-olds; news reports: 10 to 14). Whether it is free and whether catch-up is offered for older girls is not stated in any primary source seen, including IG2026 and FP7.
sti.safetyNotes: Do not tell a girl over 14 she is ineligible. She should ask at a clinic.

sti.question: Can I take PrEP to prevent HIV? I'm a teenager.
sti.answer: PrEP is medicine that HIV-negative people can use to lower their risk of getting HIV. Kenya's 2026 guidelines say it is not for adolescents under 15. From age 15, a health worker can check whether it suits you. You need an HIV test first. There are now several forms, including a daily pill, a vaginal ring, and injections given every 2 or every 6 months, and a health worker will help you choose. Ask about condoms too, because PrEP does not protect against other STIs.
sti.evidenceClaim: PrEP is indicated for HIV-negative people at ongoing risk; "Adolescents under 15 years" is listed as a contraindication; eligibility requires a confirmed HIV-negative test; options are daily oral PrEP, the dapivirine vaginal ring (every 28 days), cabotegravir long-acting injection (every 8 weeks) and lenacapavir injection (every 26 weeks).
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.3.1 pp. 17 to 18; s. 1.3.3 p. 19; Table 1.15 p. 21; WHO, HIV fact sheet
sti.conditions: Not every facility offers every form. Some forms have extra conditions (kidney or liver checks). The pages read do not state the consent rule for 15- to 17-year-olds (Table 1.12 p. 17 says "national consent guidance"). "PrEP does not protect against other STIs" is not stated on the pages read; keep the WHO citation or remove the sentence.
sti.safetyNotes: Girls under 15 who are at risk should go to a clinic or youth-friendly service for other prevention options. If she may have been exposed in the last 3 days she needs PEP urgently, not PrEP.

sti.question: Can I have an STI without knowing?
sti.answer: Yes. Many STIs cause no symptoms. For example, chlamydia causes no symptoms in about 7 in 10 women, and gonorrhoea is also often symptom-free in women. If they are not treated, they can spread to the womb and tubes and later cause pain, a pregnancy outside the womb, or trouble getting pregnant. The only way to know is a test at a health facility.
sti.evidenceClaim: Genital chlamydia infection is asymptomatic in about 70% of women; gonorrhoea is often asymptomatic in women (fewer than half of infected women report symptoms); untreated infections may cause PID, ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility; laboratory testing also detects asymptomatic infection.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.5.1 p. 171; s. 3.5.2 p. 171; s. 3.3.1 p. 161
sti.conditions: The 70% figure is the guideline's figure for chlamydia in women. It is not given for other STIs. Not every untreated infection causes complications.
sti.safetyNotes: Anyone who has had sex without a condom, or whose partner may have an STI, can ask for a test at a clinic. She does not have to have symptoms.

sti.question: If a person with HIV takes their medicine, can they still pass HIV to a partner during sex?
sti.answer: Not if their viral load stays undetectable. Kenya's 2026 guidelines say that people whose blood tests show an undetectable viral load on two tests six months apart have effectively no risk of passing HIV on through sex. This is called U=U: undetectable equals untransmittable. It depends on carrying on with the medicine and the clinic's viral load tests. It does not apply in pregnancy and breastfeeding, to injecting drug use, or to needle-stick injuries.
sti.evidenceClaim: Definition: a durable undetectable viral load (two consecutive results below 200 copies/ml six months apart) means effectively no risk of sexual transmission. U=U messaging is not applicable in pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, people who inject drugs, or needle-stick injuries.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.6.5 p. 97
sti.conditions: This is about HIV only; it says nothing about other STIs. A person cannot tell her partner's viral load without the partner's own results.
sti.safetyNotes: A partner of someone with HIV can ask a clinic about testing and prevention (PrEP or PEP). For other STIs, a test is still the only way to know.

sti.question: Is vaginal discharge always a sign of an STI?
sti.answer: No. Bacterial vaginosis, the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age, is not an STI, and neither is a yeast infection (thrush). Trichomoniasis is an STI that can cause a yellow or greenish, sometimes frothy, discharge and itching, and many women who have it have no symptoms. Because these can look alike, you can't tell by yourself. A health worker can test you and tell you which it is.
sti.evidenceClaim: BV is the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age and is not an STI. Candidiasis is not an STI. About 50 to 85% of women with T. vaginalis may have no symptoms; symptomatic women usually have abnormal discharge, and about half have vulval itching, with a yellow or greenish, sometimes frothy discharge.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.5.4 p. 172; s. 3.5.5 p. 172; s. 3.5.6 p. 173
sti.conditions: No description of normal discharge is given because none was found in the pages read. No treatments are given. This overlaps with the "discharge" gap topic, so the gynaecologist should approve it as the answer or replace it.
sti.safetyNotes: Lower belly pain, fever or pain during sex needs a visit soon. A girl who may be pregnant should be seen before taking any treatment.

sti.question: How do I get tested for HIV, and can I test myself?
sti.answer: You can be tested at a health facility, and a health worker should ask for your consent first. Kenya's guidelines also approve HIV self-test kits, where you collect your own sample (from your mouth or a drop of blood) and read the result yourself. If a self-test shows a positive result, it must be confirmed at a health facility with the national tests. If you test negative, a health worker can talk to you about ways to stay protected.
sti.evidenceClaim: HIV testing is offered with informed consent. HIV self-testing uses Ministry of Health-approved kits (oral or blood-based) and is particularly effective for reaching adolescents; a reactive self-test must be confirmed through the national testing algorithm. HIV-negative clients are linked to prevention services.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.1.1 p. 1; s. 1.1.3 p. 2
sti.conditions: The pages read do not state where to buy self-test kits, what they cost, or any age limit; no cost or "free" claim is made. A recent exposure can be missed by an early test (see NEW-S-10).
sti.safetyNotes: If a self-test is reactive, she should go to a facility for confirmation and support, not decide on her own. A recent exposure within 72 hours needs PEP urgently (see NEW-S-06).

sti.question: How soon after sex can an HIV test tell me if I have HIV?
sti.answer: Not straight away. After HIV gets into the body there is a "window period" before a test can detect it, and different tests detect it at different times, so an early negative result may not be reliable. A health worker will tell you when to test again. If a result is unclear, Kenya's guidelines say to test again after 14 days. After a possible exposure, check-up tests are repeated at 28 days and at 12 weeks.
sti.evidenceClaim: The window period is the time between exposure and detectable antibodies; different tests detect at different stages. Inconclusive results are retested after 14 days. After PEP, HIV testing is repeated at 28 days and 12 weeks; blood or organ donation is avoided until confirmed HIV-negative at 12 weeks.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.1.7 Table 1.6 p. 12; s. 1.2.4 p. 16; s. 1.2.5 p. 16
sti.conditions: No single number of days is given for when a test becomes reliable. The 28-day and 12-week schedule is the PEP follow-up schedule, not a general rule for all tests.
sti.safetyNotes: A possible exposure within the last 3 days is urgent: go to a facility about PEP (see NEW-S-06). Use condoms until the result is confirmed.

sti.question: What is pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
sti.answer: PID is an infection of the womb, tubes and the area around them. It is usually caused by STIs that were not treated, such as chlamydia and gonorrhoea. The signs can be mild or missing, so it is often missed. Pelvic or lower belly pain is the main sign, and fever or unusual discharge can come with it. Treatment that is delayed can leave lasting damage to the tubes and make it harder to get pregnant. See a health worker soon if you have lower belly pain, and go to hospital urgently for severe pelvic pain or a high fever.
sti.evidenceClaim: PID is an inflammatory disorder of the upper genital tract commonly caused by untreated chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomonas and Mycoplasma genitalium; symptoms can be subtle or absent; delay contributes to complications; diagnosis is based on pelvic or abdominal pain with tenderness, and fever and purulent discharge add to the picture; severe pelvic pain or high fever (above 38 degrees) are criteria for hospital referral. Complications include ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.6 pp. 178-179; s. 3.5.1 p. 171
sti.conditions: Treatment details are not included. The referral list in the guideline is for clinicians; the "go to hospital urgently" wording here is a simplified version for lay readers.
sti.safetyNotes: Severe pelvic pain can also be an ectopic pregnancy or appendicitis, so it should never be treated at home.

sti.question: What are genital warts, and can I prevent them?
sti.answer: Genital warts are small growths on or around the genitals or the anus, caused mostly by two types of HPV (types 6 and 11). Some are visible and some are inside the vagina or anus. They can pass to a partner, and condoms help reduce the spread. A health worker should look at any new growth, because other conditions can look similar. The HPV vaccine is very effective at preventing genital warts. HPV that causes no signs usually clears by itself.
sti.evidenceClaim: Anogenital warts are largely caused by HPV genotypes 6 and 11; may be internal; highly infectious to partners, and condoms help reduce transmission; examination is needed to rule out other causes; subclinical genital HPV infection typically clears spontaneously; the quadrivalent or nonavalent HPV vaccine is highly effective for preventing anogenital warts.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.9 p. 182
sti.conditions: No treatments are given. Whether and where a girl can get the vaccine is not stated here (see NEW-S-03, still unverified).
sti.safetyNotes: She should see a health worker for any growth rather than trying home treatments.

sti.question: I have painful sores or blisters on my genitals. Could it be herpes or syphilis?
sti.answer: It could be. Painful blisters or sores, with itching or burning when you pass urine, can be genital herpes, which can come back. Syphilis and other infections can also cause genital sores, and sometimes more than one infection is present. Some sores are not from STIs at all, for example a yeast infection or an injury. A health worker can test you and tell you which it is, so go to a clinic rather than treating it yourself.
sti.evidenceClaim: Genital ulcers can have more than one infectious cause (for example herpes and syphilis); genital herpes presents with painful vesicles or ulcers, itching, burning, dysuria and recurrent outbreaks; some genital lesions are not sexually transmitted (yeast, trauma and others); diagnosis uses tests such as PCR.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.4 and Table 3.8 p. 164
sti.conditions: No treatments or doses are given. Whether herpes can be cured is not stated in the pages read, so the answer does not say.
sti.safetyNotes: Sores plus fever, or large painful swellings in the groin, need a visit soon.

sti.question: I have itching in my pubic hair or private area. Could it be lice or scabies?
sti.answer: It could be. Pubic lice are tiny insects that live in pubic hair and usually pass on through sexual contact. A health worker can see the lice and their eggs on the hair. Scabies is a skin condition caused by tiny mites that makes the skin very itchy. In adults it is often caught through sex, but this is not always so. Itching can also have other causes, such as thrush. Both lice and scabies can be treated, so see a health worker rather than guessing.
sti.evidenceClaim: "Pediculosis pubis is caused by the parasite Phthirus pubis and is usually transmitted by sexual contact" / "The clinical diagnosis is based on typical symptoms of itching in the pubic region, lice and nits can be observed on pubic hair." / "Scabies is a skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, which causes pruritus." / "Scabies among adults is frequently sexually acquired, although scabies among children usually is not."
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.10.1 Pediculosis Pubis, p. 184; s. 3.10.2 Scabies, p. 185
sti.conditions: The guideline lists treatments (creams, lotions, tablets); none are named. "Thrush" and other causes of itching come from IG2026 s. 3.5.6 (p. 173), where candidiasis is described as "not an STI" (see NEW-S-08). Do not tell a girl that scabies means she has had sex: among children it usually is not sexually acquired.
sti.safetyNotes: If itching is with sores, unusual discharge or pain, she should see a health worker. If she says she was forced, route to the existing help reply (not a topic for this entry).

sti.question: Can I catch hepatitis B from sex, and how can I prevent it?
sti.answer: Hepatitis B is a virus that harms the liver. Kenya's 2026 guideline says it spreads through contact with infected blood or other body fluids, mainly through sex, sharing needles, needle-stick injuries, and from an infected mother to her baby at birth. Vaccination is the main way to prevent it, along with safe healthcare practices. Signs can include yellow skin or eyes, dark urine and tiredness. Ask a health worker whether you are vaccinated and whether you should be tested.
sti.evidenceClaim: "Hepatitis B is transmitted horizontally through exposures to infected blood or other body fluids, primarily via sexual contact, sharing needles, occupational exposure (like needle stick injuries), and vertically from an infected mother to her infant during birth." / Prevention: "Hepatitis B birth dose and routine immunization" (Table 4.2). / Features: "Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)", "Dark-coloured urine", fatigue. / FP7 p. 110: contraceptives "Do not protect against STIs, including hepatitis B and HIV. Individuals at risk should use condoms".
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 4.6.2 p. 192; s. 4.4 Table 4.2 and s. 4.5 p. 189; Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), p. 110
sti.conditions: The pages read do not give the vaccine schedule or catch-up rules for adolescents, so none is stated. IG2026 p. 57 says the hepatitis B vaccine is for "newborns and high-risk groups" (in a section on people living with HIV); whether a teenager is eligible needs a clinician. Hepatitis A, C and E are not covered.
sti.safetyNotes: Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or stomach pain need a health worker soon. She should not assume she is protected.

sti.question: Could a painless sore or a rash on my palms be syphilis?
sti.answer: It could. Kenya's 2026 guideline says early syphilis causes a painless sore, usually at the place where the infection got in (the genitals, anus or mouth), about 3 weeks after exposure. Because it does not hurt, it can be missed. Weeks later, about 6 to 8 weeks after the sore, it can cause a skin rash, especially on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Syphilis can be found with a blood test and cured with antibiotics, so see a health worker rather than waiting for it to go away.
sti.evidenceClaim: Primary syphilis (table cells, read as fragments): "Painless chancre at" / "site of inoculation" (genital, anal, or oral) / "~3 weeks after" exposure. Secondary syphilis: "Skin rash, especially" / "on palms and soles" / "~6-8 weeks after". Diagnosis by serological testing (RPR/VDRL, then a treponemal test). WHO: syphilis is curable.
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.4 Table 3.8, p. 166 (primary) and p. 167 (secondary); WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet
sti.conditions: Treatment drugs are not named. The guideline's blood-test details are not explained. Other conditions cause sores (herpes, yeast, injury; s. 3.4 p. 164, see NEW-S-13), so a sore does not by itself mean syphilis. "Curable" rests on WHO, as in NEW-S-02.
sti.safetyNotes: Syphilis in pregnancy affects the baby (not covered here); a pregnant girl with a sore should see a health worker without delay.

sti.question: If I have an STI, does my partner need treatment too?
sti.answer: Yes. Kenya's guidelines say that people who are diagnosed with an STI should be encouraged to tell their sexual partners, and that partners should receive testing and treatment so the infection is not passed back and forth. A health worker can help, for example by notifying your partner for you or giving you a referral.
sti.evidenceClaim: "Implement strategies to encourage individuals diagnosed with STIs to" [...] "inform their sexual partners." [...] "diagnosed individuals receive appropriate testing and treatment to reduce" [...] "the risk of re-infection and further transmission" [...] "Encourage and assist with partner notification through patient referral,"
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), STI prevention approaches table, p. 157; STI case management steps, p. 162
sti.conditions: The guidelines are written for health workers. Whether a partner can be treated without being seen is not explained here.
sti.safetyNotes: If she is afraid to tell a partner because of violence, she should talk to a health worker; call 1195, 999 or 112 if in danger.

sti.question: I have itching, burning and a thick white discharge. Could it be a yeast infection?
sti.answer: It could be. Kenya's guidelines describe a yeast infection (vaginal candidiasis) as causing itching or burning of the vulva, soreness, and a thick white or creamy discharge that is often like curds. It is not an STI, but its signs look like some STIs, and the same signs can also be caused by other infections, so it needs to be checked. Wet pads can encourage fungal infections like this, so change pads regularly. See a health worker for a test and treatment.
sti.evidenceClaim: "It is therefore not an STI" [...] "Candidiasis presents with pruritus or a burning sensation of the vulva and vaginal soreness or irritation" [...] "it characteristically is curdy, white or creamy and thick" [...] "Wet pads can cause skin irritation and encourage fungal infections like candidiasis"
sti.source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), "Candidiasis", p. 173; Kenya MoH and MoE, Menstrual Hygiene Management in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Potential Health Risks Due to Poor Hygiene During Menstruation", p. 19
sti.conditions: The guidelines are written for health workers, and the treatment is not given to the girl here. The answer does not tell her to treat herself.
sti.safetyNotes: Lower belly pain, a fever, sores or bleeding after sex needs a visit soon. See NEW-S-01.

pregnancy.question: Do I have to get a pelvic exam right away at my first visit?
pregnancy.answer: No — youth-friendly facilities should let you delay pelvic exams and blood tests until you're ready, while still addressing your immediate needs another way.
pregnancy.evidenceClaim: YFS facilities must offer options to delay pelvic exams and blood tests until the client is psychologically/emotionally prepared, alongside alternative ways to meet immediate needs.
pregnancy.source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Ch. 3 §3.3, p. 18
pregnancy.conditions: 2005 document — flag for domain expert to confirm still standard practice.

pregnancy.question: Can I stay in school if I'm pregnant, and can I go back after the baby?
pregnancy.answer: Under Kenya's 2020 national school re-entry guidelines, a pregnant learner is allowed to stay in school for as long as possible and to sit national exams if her health allows. After delivery she is re-admitted to the same class she was in before. The guidelines give the return time as six months after delivery and also as the start of the next calendar year, so ask your school's guidance and counselling teacher what applies to you.
pregnancy.evidenceClaim: A pregnant learner shall be allowed to remain in school as long as possible and to sit national exams if her health permits; after delivery she is re-admitted to the same class unconditionally.
pregnancy.source: Ministry of Education, Kenya, National Guidelines for School Re-Entry in Early Learning and Basic Education (2020), Section 3.2
pregnancy.conditions: The guidelines state the return both as six months after delivery and as the start of the next calendar year, which can differ. These are national guidelines; practice in schools varies.
pregnancy.safetyNotes: If a school refuses, she can ask the guidance and counselling teacher. A verified escalation route was not found.

pregnancy.question: What warning signs in pregnancy mean I should go to hospital right away?
pregnancy.answer: Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook lists these warning signs: vaginal bleeding, severe stomach pain, the baby moving less or not at all, fits, fever, a severe headache, waters breaking, and swelling of the face and hands. If you have any of them, go to a health facility straight away.
pregnancy.evidenceClaim: The handbook lists these danger signs and advises being prepared to seek skilled care at a health facility for any of them.
pregnancy.source: Kenya MoH, Mother & Child Health Handbook (Afya ya Mama na Mtoto), revised 2020
pregnancy.conditions: A lay list from the handbook, not a clinical triage protocol. An earlier (2016) copy lists a different set of signs, so use the 2020 edition.
pregnancy.safetyNotes: Any of these signs means going to the nearest health facility immediately. She should not wait or treat at home.

pregnancy.question: Do I need iron and folic acid tablets in pregnancy, and what should I eat?
pregnancy.answer: Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook says to take iron and folic acid supplements every day throughout pregnancy and to eat at least 5 of the 10 food groups each day. The clinic gives you the tablets. If you feel very tired, look pale or get breathless, tell the clinic.
pregnancy.evidenceClaim: Take iron and folic acid supplements every day throughout pregnancy and eat at least 5 of the 10 food groups every day.
pregnancy.source: Kenya MoH, Mother & Child Health Handbook (2020); Kenya MoH, Basic Obstetric Protocols, 1st ed. (2026)
pregnancy.conditions: The dose is for clinicians to prescribe and is not given here. Side effects were not found in a source. The WHO iron and folic acid guideline (2012) could not be opened.
pregnancy.safetyNotes: Tiredness with a pale look or breathlessness may be anaemia and needs a clinic visit.

pregnancy.question: How can I know if I am pregnant or not, and how do I get a pregnancy test?
pregnancy.answer: The way to find out is a urine pregnancy test. Kenya's guidelines say that when a period is late, irregular or you are not sure, a urine pregnancy test should be done. Ask a health worker or a youth-friendly clinic for one. Until you have a test result, you cannot be sure you are not pregnant. Use a condom or avoid sex until your period comes or the result is confirmed.
pregnancy.evidenceClaim: "if uncertain, irregular, or delayed then a urine pregnancy test should be performed" (IG2026, p. 29). "If pregnancy testing is not available, counsel the client to use barrier methods or abstain from intercourse until her menses occur or pregnancy is confirmed" (FP7, p. 45). "Pregnancy cannot completely be ruled out using the checklist" (FP7, p. 45).
pregnancy.source: Kenya MoH, HIV/STI Guidelines (IG2026), p. 29; Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guidelines for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (FP7), p. 45. Both quotes were found by exact text search; page numbers are printed pages and should be re-checked in the PDFs.
pregnancy.conditions: Both sources are written for health workers, not for girls. Neither says how soon after sex or a missed period a test is reliable, so no timing is given. The line "ask a health worker or a youth-friendly clinic for one" is not stated in these pages; it is a referral note for the clinician to confirm. FP7 p. 45 lists situations where a provider can be reasonably sure a client is not pregnant (for example a negative test and no unprotected sex in 3 weeks). That is a provider screening tool and is deliberately NOT turned into advice to the girl.
pregnancy.safetyNotes: Never tell her she is not pregnant. If she may have been raped or forced, route to the help reply (1195, 999, 112). Possible pregnancy with severe pain or heavy bleeding needs a facility visit. Held-topic group C should still send late-period and "am I pregnant" queries to a health worker; this entry would answer the "how do I get a test" wording only if the clinicians and Mr. Ouma agree it should replace or sit beside the held reply.

pregnancy.question: How many antenatal clinic visits do I need, and what happens at the first one?
pregnancy.answer: Go to the clinic as soon as you can. Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook says to go for antenatal care as soon as possible and to attend 8 times during the pregnancy, and WHO also recommends a minimum of eight contacts. At the first visit the health worker examines you and checks your blood, urine and blood sugar, and offers testing for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis. If you have a question, the handbook says to ask a health worker or a community health volunteer without any hesitation.
pregnancy.evidenceClaim: "Go for ANC visit as soon as possible and attend 8 times during the pregnancy" [...] "PHYSICAL EXAMINATION [1st Visit]" [...] "Triple testing (HIV/Syphilis/Hepatitis)" [...] "If you have any question, please ask a health worker or a Community Health Volunteer (CHV) without any hesitation" [...] "A minimum of eight contacts are recommended to reduce perinatal mortality and improve women’s experience of care."
pregnancy.source: Kenya MoH, Mother and Child Health Handbook (2020), pp. 1, 8 and 14 (page numbers from a web summary of the PDF); WHO, Recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience (2016), news release of 7 Nov 2016
pregnancy.conditions: The quotes were taken from a web summary of the handbook and WHO guidance; the medic checked the entry against the sources on 22 Oct 2026. Page numbers are from the summary. The handbook is about 'ANC contacts' counted from the first visit. It does not say what is done at the other visits in the pages read.
pregnancy.safetyNotes: Bleeding, severe pain, a severe headache, fever or the baby moving less means going to a facility at once (see NEW-P-02).

pregnancy.question: How do I prepare for giving birth?
pregnancy.answer: Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook has a birth plan, which a health worker fills in with you during your antenatal visits. It covers where you will give birth, who will assist you, how you will get to the health facility, who could donate blood if needed, and how you will pay for the birth. The handbook also says to have transport ready to reach the facility and to prepare money, a birth companion and an emergency kit. Talk to a health worker at your antenatal visits to make your plan.
pregnancy.evidenceClaim: "Birth Plan: Preparing for a safe and healthy childbirth" [...] "Financial plan for childbirth" [...] "Ensure transport to the health facility is available (Birth preparedness; money, birth companion, emergency kit)"
pregnancy.source: Kenya MoH, Mother and Child Health Handbook (2020), Birth Plan, p. 1; birth preparedness, p. 4 (page numbers from a web summary of the PDF)
pregnancy.conditions: The quotes were taken from a web summary of the handbook; the medic checked the entry against the sources on 22 Oct 2026. The handbook sentences about who 'could donate blood' and 'who will assist you' are paraphrases of the birth-plan headings and need checking. It does not say what to pack in the emergency kit.
pregnancy.safetyNotes: Labour pains, waters breaking, bleeding or the baby not moving means going to a health facility straight away (see NEW-P-02).

general.question: Will the clinic tell my parents what I talked to them about?
general.answer: Youth-friendly health services are expected to keep what you share confidential, including from parents — except in specific situations where the law requires disclosure, which staff should explain to you clearly.
general.evidenceClaim: Providers must maintain confidentiality and not leak information to parents; legal exceptions exist but aren't specified in this source.
general.source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Ch. 3 §3.2–3.3, pp. 16–17
general.conditions: Exact legal exceptions not established by this source — flag if a user's question implies a specific legal scenario.

general.question: What age counts as "youth" or "adolescent" for these services?
general.answer: Kenyan services define adolescents as 10–19, youth as 15–24, and young people as 10–24 — these terms are often used interchangeably.
general.evidenceClaim: Age range definitions for target populations in Kenya.
general.source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Ch. 1 §1.1.2, p. 2

general.question: Is my period normal, and when should I see a health worker?
general.answer: Periods vary from girl to girl. Kenya's school handbook says some girls have cycles of 21 days and others 35 days, and bleeding usually lasts 2 to 7 days, with about 5 days the average. In the first years after periods start they may not be regular. WHO says bleeding that is unpredictable, infrequent, very painful or heavy, or that stops you doing normal activities, could point to an underlying health condition, so see a health worker. A late period can have many causes, including pregnancy.
general.evidenceClaim: MHM: "Some girls menstruate every 28 days while others have longer cycles of 35 days or shorter cycles of 21 days." / "Menstruation usually last from 2-7 days with 5 days being the average length of menstrual flow." / "Menstrual cycle for the first few years is not regular for some girls." WHO: menstrual bleeding that is unpredictable, infrequent, very painful, heavy, or disrupts normal activities could suggest an underlying health condition.
general.source: Kenya MoH and MoE, Menstrual Hygiene Management in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Facts about Menstruation", p. 10; WHO, Menstrual health fact sheet
general.conditions: The handbook does not say when bleeding is too heavy or too long, or how many days late a period must be before testing. Confirm the handbook's edition and date (cover says 2020; file name says April 2022).
general.safetyNotes: Very heavy bleeding, or pain that stops usual activities, needs a facility visit. A late period should be routed to a health worker or a pregnancy test, not diagnosed (held-topic group C).

general.question: What can I do about period pain?
general.answer: Many girls have period pain: WHO says more than 2 in 3 women and girls do. Kenya's school handbook suggests putting a bottle of hot water on your tummy, doing some exercise such as skipping or swimming, drinking plenty of water and eating a healthy, balanced diet. If you want a painkiller, ask a pharmacist or health worker which one is safe for you. See a health worker if the pain goes on for a long time or stops your usual activities.
general.evidenceClaim: MHM: "Place hot water in a bottle on the abdomen to relieve cramps." / "Physical exercises such as swimming, running, jogging, skipping, hula hoop." / "Eat healthy balanced diet all the time." / "Drink plenty of water." / "Please visit a doctor if you are experiencing discomforts for a longer period of time." WHO: more than 2 out of 3 women and girls have pain with menstrual bleeding. NHS: see a GP if pain stops usual daily activities.
general.source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM Handbook for Teachers, "Pain Management of Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS)", p. 20; WHO, Menstrual health fact sheet; NHS, Period pain (UK)
general.conditions: The handbook gives no painkiller advice; the painkiller line rests on the NHS source from the 6 Oct draft. No doses. Some painkillers are unsuitable for some people (for example with stomach ulcers or asthma), which was not verified here.
general.safetyNotes: Severe or worsening pelvic pain needs a facility visit. Pain with a late period could be pregnancy-related, so it should not be called just a period.

general.question: How do I manage my period hygienically?
general.answer: Kenya's school handbook gives these tips: change your pad or other menstrual product regularly, wash your hands with soap and clean water before and after changing it, bathe or shower at least once a day, and change your underwear every day or when it is soiled. Wash the outside of the vagina with water only, and do not put soap, deodorant or liquids inside the vagina. Wipe from front to back after using the toilet.
general.evidenceClaim: "Taking a bath or shower at least once a day." / "Using of a clean undergarment and changing them regularly, a minimum of every day or when soiled." / "Changing of menstrual product and material regularly during menstruation." / "Ensuring hand washing with soap and clean water before and after changing the product." / "Washing the vagina with water only! … the vagina has its own self-cleaning mechanism. An external cleaning agent or deodorant should not be used and too much soap can cause itching." / "Wiping from front to back following urination or defecation to avoid infections." / "Avoiding douching…" / "Infrequent change of menstrual products can cause urinary tract infections (UTIs) and reproductive tract infections (RTIs)."

general.conditions: The handbook gives no number of hours between changes. Tampon and cup advice, including toxic shock syndrome (pp. 19 to 20), is not included without a clinician.
general.safetyNotes: Unusual discharge, itching or burning should be seen at a clinic. Toxic shock signs (sudden high fever, rash, vomiting, confusion) are an emergency but the source puts them under tampon use, so they are held out of this entry.

general.question: What changes happen to my body at puberty, and when does my first period come?
general.answer: The first sign of puberty in most girls is breast 'buds', followed by body hair and a growth spurt. Kenya's school handbook says a girl's first period happens between the ages of 9 and 17, and some girls get theirs as early as 9. Periods may be irregular for the first few years. Timing varies from girl to girl, so if you are worried about your development, talk to a health worker.
general.evidenceClaim: AAP: breast buds are the earliest sign of puberty. MHM: the first period occurs "between 9-17 years"; "Some girls have their first menstruation as early as nine years of age."; "Menstrual cycle for the first few years is not regular for some girls."

general.conditions: The handbook's own diagram on p. 8 says an egg matures "between the ages of 8 and 19 years"; the 9 to 17 range is used. The AAP source is American. KDHS 2022 was not opened.
general.safetyNotes: If there are no signs of puberty, or no period well past the usual ages, talk to a health worker. No verified age thresholds for worry were found.

general.question: What does a youth-friendly health service offer, and what should I expect?
general.answer: Kenya's 2025 family planning guideline says services for adolescents and youth should be equitable, accessible, acceptable, appropriate and effective. In practice that means services should be affordable, open at convenient times such as after school and on weekends, give you information you can understand, and keep what you say confidential, including when you register and in your records. You should be able to speak to a provider in a place where no one can see or hear you.
general.evidenceClaim: "Healthcare providers … shall provide adolescent and youth-friendly services that are equitable, accessible, acceptable, appropriate and effective…" / "SRH services must be affordable and available to all adolescents and youth." / "…made obtainable during convenient hours, including after school or work and during weekends and holidays…" / "Confidentiality should be maintained at all times, including during registration, consultation, record-keeping and disclosure." / "The point of service delivery should be located in a place that affords auditory and visual privacy." / "The services should offer appropriate information that will be understood by the client…"

general.conditions: These are standards for how services should be delivered; a given facility may not meet them. The pages describe family planning services; they do not list a full package of services, facility types or helplines, so none is named. The 2005 and 2016 YFS guidelines are not used. The same section (p. 25) says adolescents under 18 give assent and a guardian gives consent for FP services; this entry does not state a consent rule.
general.safetyNotes: Urgent symptoms (heavy bleeding, severe pain, possible pregnancy) need prompt care.

general.question: Why do I feel tired, moody or get pimples before my period?
general.answer: That could be premenstrual syndrome (PMS), a group of symptoms linked to your cycle that start 1 to 2 weeks before your period. Kenya's school handbook lists tender breasts, pimples, tiredness, trouble sleeping, headache or backache, bloating, changes in appetite, and mood swings or feeling tearful. For some girls PMS is just a monthly bother, and for others it is so strong that it is hard to get through the day. It goes away when your periods stop, for example during pregnancy. If it is making daily life hard, or you feel very sad or anxious, see a health worker.
general.evidenceClaim: "PMS symptoms occur 1 to 2 weeks before your menstruation or monthly bleeding starts." / "For some people, PMS is just a monthly bother. For others, it may be so severe that it makes it hard to even get through the day." / Symptoms listed: "Acne/pimples", "Swollen or tender breasts", "Feeling tired", "Trouble sleeping", "Headache or backache", "Tension, irritability, mood swings, or crying spells", "Anxiety or depression". / "PMS goes away when your monthly periods stop, such as when you get pregnant or go through menopause."

general.conditions: The handbook does not say what counts as severe or when to see a health worker for PMS (the "visit a doctor" tip on p. 20 is about long-lasting discomfort). Late-period and pregnancy questions go to the held-topic rules. See NEW-G-02 for cramps.
general.safetyNotes: Persistent low mood or anxiety that does not go away needs a health worker or counsellor. If she says she wants to harm herself, the Safety Net reply applies, not this entry.

general.question: What can I use during my period: pads, tampons or a cup?
general.answer: Kenya's school handbook lists four choices: disposable pads, reusable pads, tampons and menstrual cups. The choice depends on what you prefer, whether you have water and a place to dispose of products, and what suits your underwear. Disposable pads are easy to use but cost more and are not always available. Reusable pads cost less but need water and somewhere private to wash and dry them; if they are not cleaned well they can cause infections, and you should not share them. Tampons and cups go inside the vagina, and need instructions before you use them. A tampon left in too long can cause a serious illness called toxic shock syndrome, so change it often. Keep products in a clean, cool, dry place.

general.question: How do I dispose of a used pad safely?
general.answer: Kenya's school handbook says to wrap the used pad in paper, put it in a dustbin and close the lid. Keep period waste separate from other rubbish by using a sanitary bin where there is one. Throwing pads in pit latrines or toilets is shown as the wrong way, because it blocks drains and can pollute water. If there is no bin, wrap the pad and keep it until you can dispose of it safely.

general.question: What is a period, and why does it happen?
general.answer: A period is a regular discharge of blood and tissue from the lining of the womb (uterus), which comes out through the vagina. Kenya's school handbook explains it like this: usually one egg matures in each cycle and travels from the ovary down the fallopian tube, and meanwhile the womb lining gets thicker. If the egg is not fertilised, the body sheds the lining as blood, and that is your period. If the egg is fertilised, the lining provides a home for a growing baby. A period is a normal part of growing up. It starts at puberty and stops later in life at menopause.

general.safetyNotes: None beyond NEW-G-01 (when to see a health worker).

general.question: Is having a period dirty, shameful or a sickness?
general.answer: No. Kenya's school handbook says menstruation is a normal and natural part of growing up. It is not a sickness, an illness, a disease or an infection, and it is not harmful, a curse, dirty, shameful or unclean. It is nothing to be ashamed of.
general.evidenceClaim: "Menstruation is not:" [...] "Sickness, illness, disease, infection," [...] "harmful, a curse, dirty, shameful, or" [...] "A normal and natural part of" [...] "biological maturity." [...] "something to be ashamed of"

general.conditions: This is about stigma and myths. It does not cover painful or heavy periods; those are in NEW-G-01 and NEW-G-02.
general.safetyNotes: Very heavy bleeding or pain that stops usual activities needs a health worker (see NEW-G-01).

general.question: Can I get pregnant once I have started my periods?
general.answer: Yes. Kenya's school handbook says menstruation is a sign that a girl can become pregnant. Once your periods have started, sex without protection can lead to pregnancy. A health worker can explain how to prevent pregnancy.

general.source: Kenya MoH and MoE, Menstrual Hygiene Management in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Facts about Menstruation", p. 10
general.conditions: The handbook does not say when in the cycle pregnancy is possible, so the answer does not either. The second and third sentences are an explanation and a referral note that are not in the page.
general.safetyNotes: If she may already be pregnant, see a health worker (NEW-P-04).

general.question: Is it normal that I have not started my periods yet?
general.answer: Girls start at different ages. Kenya's school handbook says the first period usually comes between 9 and 17 years of age, and some girls start as early as nine. Everyone goes through puberty differently, and in the first few years periods may not come regularly. If you are worried, talk to a health worker or a teacher you trust.
general.evidenceClaim: "occurring between 9-17 years" [...] "menstruation as early as nine years" [...] "years is not regular for some girls" [...] "Everyone experiences puberty differently"
general.source: Kenya MoH and MoE, Menstrual Hygiene Management in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Menstruation and Semenarche", p. 8; "Facts about Menstruation", p. 10

general.question: What should I not use as a pad during my period?
general.answer: Kenya's school handbook strongly discourages using cow dung, mud, leaves, tissue paper, dirty pieces of cloth, animal skin, pieces of mattress or blanket, or chicken and bird feathers, because they are unsafe and unhygienic. It also discourages sitting on soil or sand during your period. Pads, reusable pads, tampons and menstrual cups are the products the handbook describes.

general.conditions: The handbook does not say what to do if a girl cannot afford pads, so the answer does not either. It does not say whether clean cloth is acceptable.
general.safetyNotes: Itching, a bad smell or pain after using any material should be seen by a health worker.

general.question: What can I do about itching, a rash or a bad smell during my period?
general.answer: Kenya's school handbook links itching and rashes to how pads are used and washed. Wet pads can irritate the skin and encourage fungal infections, and using dirty period products can lead to infections of the vagina. The handbook advises you to bath or shower at least once a day, change into clean underwear every day or when it is soiled, change your pad or other product regularly, wash your hands with soap and water before and after changing it, and clean the outside of your genitals often. Wash the vagina with water only: it cleans itself, and deodorants and too much soap can cause itching. Wipe from front to back. Some pads contain perfume and chemicals that can cause rashes. See a health worker if it does not go away.

general.question: Can I swim, run or play sports when I am on my period?
general.answer: Kenya's school handbook lists physical exercise such as swimming, running, jogging, skipping and hula hoop as ways to ease period discomfort, along with a hot water bottle on the tummy to relieve cramps, a healthy diet and drinking plenty of water. If you use a tampon or cup, remember to change or empty it on time, and see a health worker if you get a sudden high fever, a rash or vomiting.

general.question: Is it normal to feel sick, vomit, have diarrhoea or a headache around my period?
general.answer: It can be. Kenya's school handbook lists an upset stomach, bloating, nausea, vomiting, constipation or diarrhoea, headache or backache among the symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS), which begins 1 to 2 weeks before your period. It says symptoms differ from girl to girl and are strong enough in some girls to make it hard to get through the day. To ease them the handbook suggests a hot water bottle on the tummy, exercise, a healthy diet and plenty of water. Visit a doctor if the discomfort goes on for a long time.
